title: Collaborative AI agents for autonomous experimental research with solid-state quantum spins
authors: El Mustapha Mansouri, Eikichi Kimura, Masato Koga, Keigo Arai
abstract: An autonomous research laboratory could conduct an entire study, from formulating questions to preparing manuscripts. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers one route towards this goal. Recent AI systems take on several research roles, but may draw conclusions that the evidence does not support. Here, we present an autonomous research laboratory in which agents based on large language models assess one another's work and can stop or redirect investigations. They can generate and reject research questions, require separate theoretical checks and conduct experiments designed to challenge their claims. We demonstrate these capabilities by investigating ensembles of quantum spins in diamond. The agents derived the minimum number of calibration settings needed to predict responses to a defined family of microwave pulse sequences. They checked the result computationally and designed experiments to distinguish competing predictions. An initial experiment agreed with the theoretical predictions, but repeated reference measurements showed that the signal was drifting during data collection. The agents therefore treated the result as inconclusive and revised the measurement protocol without relaxing the acceptance criteria. The revised experiment met those criteria and supported the theoretical predictions. This study demonstrates that collaborating AI agents can select research questions, derive theoretical results and test their predictions experimentally.
summary: This work presents an autonomous research laboratory powered by collaborative AI agents that tackles a problem in quantum spin physics using NV centers in diamond. The agents successfully derived a theoretical minimum for required calibration measurements and then iteratively refined an experimental protocol to validate this theory against real-world signal drift. It demonstrates a powerful paradigm for AI-driven scientific discovery.
main_problem: Developing an autonomous research laboratory using AI agents to conduct a complete scientific study, while ensuring conclusions are rigorously supported by evidence and experimental validation.
main_result: Collaborating AI agents successfully selected, challenged, and substantiated a new physical claim regarding quantum spins through iterative theoretical derivation and experimental refinement.
method: The study employs a multi-agent system where specialized AI agents (PI, computational researcher, experimentalist) interact to propose, test, and revise hypotheses regarding quantum spin ensembles.
model_or_system: The physical system investigated is an ensemble of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond, whose collective quantum spin response is probed using controlled microwave-pulse sequences.
key_observables: Signal drift during data collection, calibration ambiguity, and the final measured fluorescence signal supporting the derived calibration law.
important_parameters: The minimum number of calibration settings required to predict ensemble responses, which was determined to be $L^2 + 1$ for sequences of length $L$.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that the system can be modeled by a law derived from the agents, and that iterative self-correction (e.g., revising protocols after drift) is possible.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the scientific workflow and coordination among the various AI roles; Figure 2 details the process of research question selection and rejection by the Principal Investigator agent.
paper_structure: The paper follows a cycle: agents propose questions $ightarrow$ theoretical derivation (finding the minimum calibration law) $ightarrow$ computational verification $ightarrow$ initial experiment (finding drift) $ightarrow$ protocol revision $ightarrow$ final successful experiment supporting the theory.
why_interesting: The integration of advanced AI agent frameworks directly into the experimental loop for quantum physics provides a blueprint for accelerating discovery in complex quantum systems, moving beyond simple data analysis.

Figure 2: How the accepted proposal emerged. (a) Every proposal at its delivery time, marked by the PI’s decision. The dashed line marks when the repeatedly rejected idea families were listed in the proposers’ instructions. The ringed proposal was rejected but named the best seed, and its revision was accepted. (b) Reasons for rejecting 75 proposals, in four categories: logically invalid (false or invalid claims, overclaims), already known, not significant (no core theorem, trivial, renamed mathematics, too narrow) and no feasible test. Dark bars count the decisive reason and light bars every reason cited.

Figure 3: Discovery and verification of a minimal ensemble-calibration law. (a) The revised proposal supplied an upper bound of 8L2 + 6L + 1 calibrations, which the principal-investigator agent refined to the exact necessary-and-sufficient count L2 + 1 under persistent pulse errors. (b) Calibration requirements compared with the number of possible sequences for five phase choices per pulse, with the first phase fixed. (c) Certified prediction-error and calibration-ambiguity bounds under hidden phase rotations, relative to photon-counting noise.
